input:
Pervaporation is an attractive membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed is brought into contact with one side of a membrane while a vacuum applied to the other side draws the component that permeates through the membrane in the form of a vapour. In the study reported here, a polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane were evaluated side by side for the removal of water from a feed consisting of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C. Two performance measures are used throughout. The flux is the mass of material permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), and the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the corresponding ratio in the feed.

The headline results can be summarised as follows. The polymer membrane delivers the higher flux but the lower separation factor (2.1 kg m-2 h-1; 120), whereas the zeolite membrane delivers the lower flux but a considerably higher separation factor (1.2 kg m-2 h-1; 420). Long-term stability draws a further distinction between the two materials: the flux of the polymer membrane fell 9% over 500 h of operation, while the flux of the zeolite membrane was unchanged over 500 h, at least within the limits of measurement error.

Taken together, the results present the familiar trade-off between throughput and selectivity. The polymer offers more throughput but less enrichment, and its advantage is eroded to some extent by the decline it exhibits during the test; the zeolite offers less throughput but more enrichment, and it maintains its performance. It should be borne in mind that only one feed composition was investigated and that no test ran beyond 500 h. This matters because flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for one and the same membrane, and it is precisely the combination of all three that determines which material is preferable in practice.
target:
Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Two membranes were compared for the removal of water from a feed of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), and the separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed.

The polymer membrane gives the higher flux and the lower separation factor (2.1 kg m-2 h-1; 120). The zeolite membrane gives the lower flux and the higher separation factor (1.2 kg m-2 h-1; 420). Stability separates the membranes further: the flux of the polymer membrane fell 9% over 500 h, and the flux of the zeolite membrane was unchanged over 500 h, within measurement error.

The comparison is a trade-off between throughput and selectivity. Neither membrane dominates: each leads on one measure and trails on the other, and the vacuum duty that drives the separation is common to both. The polymer passes more mass per unit area and enriches the permeate less, and part of its flux advantage is spent by the decline over the test period; the zeolite passes less, enriches more, and holds its flux. The scope of the comparison is one feed composition and tests that ran to 500 h at most. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the ranking of the two membranes rests on the three being measured in one test programme.
